sentences.text: The holotype skeleton contains the skull but is missing the tail and hindlimbs, yet it reveals signs of a mature, elderly individual through fused ribs, a fused shoulder girdle, rough joint surfaces, and rough armor.
In 2018, scientists estimated the total length of this animal to be six meters.
Its foot was robust and equipped with arched claws.
Another specimen, ROM 813, preserves a skullless skeleton with complete hindquarters, forelimbs, and hindlimbs, alongside skin impressions and numerous osteoderms.
The generic name Platypelta combines Greek words meaning 'wide' and 'small shield,' referring to the animal's broad osteoderms.
The species name coombsi honors Walter P. Coombs Jr., a pioneer in the study of ankylosaurs.
The holotype specimen AMNH 5337 was excavated in 1914 by Barnum Brown and Peter Kaisen in Alberta, Canada.
This specimen was found at an altitude of 667 meters within the Dinosaur Park Formation, indicating an age of about 76.8 million years.
In 2018, Penkalski named the genus Platypelta for specimens AMNH 5337 and AMNH 5403 after finding them distinct from Euoplocephalus tutus in cladistic analysis.
Platypelta is classified within the family Ankylosauridae, subfamily Ankylosaurinae, and tribe Ankylosaurini.
The parent group of Platypelta is the tribe Euoplocephalini.
Platypelta is a member of the clade Euoplocephalini, which Penkalski established as an approximate synonym of Ankylosaurini.
In the evolutionary tree, Platypelta is placed above Scolosaurus and below Dyoplosaurus.
Platypelta belongs to the class Ornithischia.
Platypelta lived during the early Late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 77.5 to 76.5 million years ago, in southern Alberta, Canada.
In 2013, Arbour and Currie suggested that AMNH 5337 and AMNH 5403 belong to Euoplocephalus, proposing that differences might result from growth and development changes.
